danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: Da Nikolaj Rostov vendte hjem til Moskva fra hæren, blev han modtaget af familien som den bedste af sønner, en helt og deres elskede Nikolenka; af slægtningene som en charmerende, tiltrækkende og høflig ung mand; af bekendtskaberne som en smuk husarløjtnant, en god danser og et af byens bedste partier.

Familien Rostov kendte alle i Moskva. Den gamle greve havde penge nok det år, da alle hans godser var blevet belånt på ny, og så Nikolaj, der anskaffede sin egen traver, de mest moderigtige ridebukser af det seneste snit — som ingen anden endnu havde i Moskva — og støvler efter seneste mode med ekstremt spidse snuder og små sølvsporer, tilbragte sin tid meget lystigt. Efter en kort tilpasningsperiode til de gamle forhold fandt Nikolaj det meget behageligt at være hjemme igen. Han følte, at han var vokset op og modnet betragteligt. Hans fortvivlelse over at dumpe i Bibelhistorie, hans lån af penge hos Gavril til en droschkekusk, hans hemmelige kys med Sonja — alt dette huskede han nu som barnagtigheder, han for længst var vokset fra. Nu var han husarløjtnant i en sølvbesnøret jakke med Skt. Georgskorset, der blev tildelt soldater for tapperhed, og i selskab med velkendte, ældre, respekterede væddeløbsmænd trænede han sin egen traver til et løb. Han kendte en dame på en af boulevarderne, som han besøgte om aftenen. Han førte mazurkaen an ved Arkharovernes bal, talte om krigen med feltmarskal Kamenski, gik i Engelske Klub og var på fortrolig fod med en oberst på fyrre, som Denisov havde introduceret ham for.

Hans lidenskab for kejseren var kølnet en smule i Moskva. Men alligevel, da han ikke så ham og ikke havde mulighed for at se ham, talte han ofte om ham og om sin kærlighed til ham og lod skinne igennem, at han ikke havde fortalt alt, og at der var noget i hans følelser for kejseren, som ikke alle kunne forstå; og med hele sin sjæl delte han den tilbedelse af kejseren, der var almindelig i Moskva, hvor man kaldte ham »den inkarnerede engel«.

Under Rostovs korte ophold i Moskva, inden han vendte tilbage til hæren, nærmede han sig ikke Sonja, men fjernede sig snarere fra hende. Hun var meget smuk og sød og tydeligvis dybt forelsket i ham, men han var i den alder, hvor der synes at være så meget, der skal gøres, at der ikke er tid til den slags ting, og en ung mand frygter at binde sig og værner om sin frihed, som han har brug for til så mange andre ting. Når han tænkte på Sonja under dette ophold i Moskva, sagde han til sig selv: »Der vil komme, og der er, mange andre sådanne piger et sted, som jeg endnu ikke kender. Der bliver tid nok til at tænke på kærlighed, når jeg vil, men nu har jeg ikke tid.« Desuden forekom det ham, at kvindeselskab var noget nær en forringelse af hans mandighed. Han gik til baller og i dameselskab med et skær af at gøre det mod sin vilje. Væddeløbene, Engelske Klub, svireture med Denisov og besøg i et bestemt hus — det var noget helt andet og fuldt passende for en flot ung husar!
I begyndelsen af marts var den gamle grev Ilja Rostov travlt optaget af at arrangere en middag til ære for fyrst Bagration i Engelske Klub.

Greven vandrede frem og tilbage i forhallen i sin slobrok og gav ordrer til klubbens forvalter og den berømte Feoktist, klubbens køkkenchef, om asparges, friske agurker, jordbær, kalvekød og fisk til denne middag. Greven havde været medlem og siddet i bestyrelsen, siden klubben blev grundlagt. Det var ham, klubben betroede arrangementet af festen til ære for Bagration, for få forstod sig så godt på at arrangere et gilde i stor og gæstfri stil, og endnu færre var villige og i stand til af egen lomme at dække, hvad der måtte mangle for festens succes. Klubbens kok og forvalter lyttede til grevens ordrer med tilfredse ansigter, for de vidste, at under ingen anden ledelse kunne de så let udtrække et godt udbytte for sig selv af en middag til flere tusinde rubler.
»Godt, og husk nu hanekamme i skildpaddesuppen, forstår I!«
»Skal vi have tre kolde retter?« spurgte kokken.
Greven overvejede.
»Færre kan vi ikke have — jo, tre ... mayonnaisen, det er den ene,« sagde han og bøjede en finger.
»Skal jeg så bestille de store sterletter?« spurgte forvalteren.

»Ja, det kan ikke undgås, hvis de ikke vil tage mindre. Åh, du godeste! Jeg glemte helt — vi mangler en forret mere. Åh, herregud!« Han greb sig til hovedet. »Hvem skaffer mig blomsterne? Dmitrij! Dmitrij! Tag af sted til vores Moskva-gods,« sagde han til sin faktotum, der dukkede op ved hans kalden. »Skynd dig og sig til Maksim, gartneren, at han skal sætte folkene i gang. Sig, at alt fra drivhusene skal bringes hertil, godt pakket ind i filt. Jeg skal have to hundrede potter her på fredag.«

Efter at have givet adskillige ordrer mere var han ved at gå ind til sin »lille grevinde« for at hvile sig, men da han huskede noget vigtigt, vendte han om igen, kaldte kokken og forvalteren tilbage og gav nye ordrer. Et let fodtrin og klirren af sporer hørtes ved døren, og den unge greve — smuk, rosenrød, med et mørkt lille overskæg, tydeligvis udhvilet og gjort endnu glattere af sit bekvemme liv i Moskva — trådte ind i stuen.

»Ak, min dreng, mit hoved er en mølle!« sagde den gamle mand med et smil, som om han var lidt forlegen over for sin søn. »Hvis du bare ville hjælpe en smule! Jeg skal også have sangere. Jeg beholder mit eget orkester, men burde vi ikke også skaffe sigøjnersangere? I militærfolk kan godt lide den slags.«
»Virkelig, far — jeg tror, fyrst Bagration ikke bekymrede sig halvt så meget før slaget ved Schön Grabern, som du gør nu,« sagde sønnen med et smil.
Den gamle greve lod, som var han vred.
»Ja, du kan sagtens snakke, men prøv det selv!«
Og greven vendte sig til kokken, der med et klogt og respektfuldt udtryk iagttog far og søn med sympatisk opmærksomhed.
»Hvad er de unge mennesker kommet til, hva', Feoktist?« sagde han. »Griner af os gamle!«
»Ja, Deres excellence, det eneste de skal er at spise en god middag, men at skaffe den til veje og servere det hele — det bekymrer de sig ikke om!«

»Netop! Netop!« udbrød greven og greb muntert sin søn om begge hænder. »Nu har jeg dig, så tag slæden med parspandet med det samme og kør til Bezukhovs og sig ham: 'Grev Ilja har sendt mig for at bede om jordbær og friske ananas.' Vi kan ikke skaffe dem andre steder. Han er ikke selv hjemme, så du må gå ind og spørge fyrstinderne; og derfra videre til Razguljaj — kusken Ipatka ved vejen — og find sigøjneren Iljusjka, ham der dansede hos grev Orlov, husker du, i den hvide kosakfrakke, og bring ham med hertil.«
»Og skal jeg tage sigøjnerpigerne med?« spurgte Nikolaj leende. »Jøsses, jøsses! ...«

I dette øjeblik trådte Anna Mikhajlovna ind i forhallen med lydløse skridt og det forretningsprægede, optagne, men ydmygt kristne udtryk, der aldrig forlod hendes ansigt. Selvom hun dagligt så greven i hans slobrok, blev han altid forlegen og bad om undskyldning for sin påklædning.

»Det gør overhovedet ikke noget, kære greve,« sagde hun og lukkede ydmygt øjnene. »Men jeg kører selv til Bezukhov. Pierre er kommet hjem, og nu kan vi få alt, hvad vi vil, fra hans drivhuse. Jeg har alligevel brug for at se ham. Han har sendt mig et brev fra Boris. Gud ske lov, Boris er nu ved staben.«
Greven var henrykt over, at Anna Mikhajlovna påtog sig et af hans ærinder, og bestilte den lille lukkede vogn til hende.
»Sig til Bezukhov, at han skal komme. Jeg skriver hans navn op. Er hans kone med ham?« spurgte han.
Anna Mikhajlovna vendte blikket mod himlen, og der lagde sig en dyb bedrøvelse over hendes ansigt.

»Ak, min kære ven, han er meget ulykkelig,« sagde hun. »Hvis det, vi hører, er sandt, er det frygteligt. Hvor lidt vi anede, da vi glædede os over hans lykke! Og en så ophøjet englesjæl som den unge Bezukhov! Ja, jeg beklager ham af hele mit hjerte og vil prøve at give ham den trøst, jeg kan.«
»Hvad er der da sket?« spurgte både den unge og den gamle Rostov.
Anna Mikhajlovna sukkede dybt.

»Dolokhov, Marja Ivanovnas søn,« sagde hun i et hemmelighedsfuldt hvisk, »har kompromitteret hende fuldstændigt, siger man. Pierre tog sig af ham, inviterede ham til sit hus i Petersborg, og nu ... hun er kommet hertil, og den vovehalsen efter hende!« sagde Anna Mikhajlovna, der ønskede at vise sin medfølelse for Pierre, men ved ufrivillige tonefald og et halvt smil forrådede sin sympati for »vovehalsen«, som hun kaldte Dolokhov. »Man siger, Pierre er helt knust af sin ulykke.«
»Jøsses, jøsses! Men sig ham alligevel, at han skal komme til klubben — det går nok over. Det bliver et storslået gilde.«

Næste dag, den tredje marts, stod kort efter klokken et to hundrede og halvtreds medlemmer af Engelske Klub og halvtreds gæster og ventede på æresgæsten og helten fra felttoget i Østrig, fyrst Bagration, til middag.

Da de første nyheder om slaget ved Austerlitz nåede Moskva, havde byen været i chok. På det tidspunkt var russerne så vant til sejre, at nogle ved nyheden om nederlaget simpelthen ikke ville tro det, mens andre søgte en ekstraordinær forklaring på en så mærkelig begivenhed. I Engelske Klub, hvor alle, der var fornemme, vigtige og velinformerede, samledes, da nyhederne begyndte at komme i december, talte ingen om krigen og det seneste slag, som om alle var enige om at tie. De toneangivende mænd — grev Rostoptjin, fyrst Jurij Dolgorukov, Valujev, grev Markov og fyrst Vjasemskij — viste sig ikke i klubben, men mødtes privat i snævre kredse, og de moskovitter, der tog andres meninger til sig — Ilja Rostov iblandt dem — stod en tid uden nogen klar holdning til krigen og uden lederskab. Moskovitterne fornemmede, at noget var galt, og at det var vanskeligt at tale om de dårlige nyheder, og så var det bedst at tie. Men efter nogen tid, ligesom nævninge kommer ud af deres rådslagning, viste de store mænd, der bestemte klubbens holdning, sig igen, og alle begyndte at tale klart og bestemt. Årsagerne til den utrolige, uhørte og umulige begivenhed — et russisk nederlag — blev fundet, alt blev klart, og i alle Moskvas kroge sagde man det samme. Årsagerne var: østrigernes forræderi, et mangelfuldt forsyningsvæsen, polakken Przebyszewskis forræderi og franskmanden Langerons, Kutuzovs uduelighed, og — det hviskede man — kejserens ungdom og uerfarenhed, der havde sat sin lid til værdiløse og ubetydelige folk. Men hæren, den russiske hær, erklærede alle, var enestående og havde udrettet tapperhedens mirakler. Soldaterne, officererne, generalerne var helte. Men helten over alle helte var fyrst Bagration, berømt for affæren ved Schön Grabern og for tilbagetrækningen fra Austerlitz, hvor han alene havde trukket sin kolonne tilbage intakt og hele dagen slået en dobbelt overlegen fjendtlig styrke tilbage. Hvad der yderligere bidrog til, at netop Bagration blev valgt som Moskvas helt, var det forhold, at han ingen forbindelser havde i byen og var en fremmed. I hans person hyldede man en jævn, kæmpende russisk soldat uden forbindelser og intriger, og en mand, der gennem erindringen om felttoget i Italien var forbundet med Suvorovs navn. Desuden var det at hylde Bagration den bedste måde at udtrykke utilfredshed med Kutuzov.

»Havde der ikke været nogen Bagration, ville man have måttet opfinde ham,« sagde vittighedsmanden Sjinsjin og parodierede Voltaires ord. Om Kutuzov talte ingen, undtagen dem, der hviskende skældte ham ud for at være en hofvejrhane og en gammel satyros.

Hele Moskva gentog fyrst Dolgorukovs udsagn: »Hvis man bliver ved med at knæde og forme, ender man med at blive tilsmurt af ler,« som en trøst for nederlaget ved minder om tidligere sejre; og Rostoptjins ord om, at franske soldater skal anspores til kamp med højtravende fraser, tyskere med logiske argumenter om, at det er farligere at flygte end at rykke frem, men at russiske soldater kun behøver at holdes tilbage! Fra alle sider hørtes nye og friske anekdoter om individuelle eksempler på heroisme fra vores officerer og menige ved Austerlitz. Én havde reddet en fane, en anden havde dræbt fem franskmænd, en tredje havde betjent fem kanoner egenhændigt. Om Berg fortalte de, der ikke kendte ham, at han, da han var såret i højre hånd, tog sablen i venstre og fortsatte fremad. Om Bolkonskij sagde man intet, og kun de, der kendte ham nøje, beklagede, at han var død så ung og havde efterladt en gravid hustru hos sin sære far.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: After returning to Moscow from the army, Nicholas Rostov was welcomed by his household as the best of sons, a hero, and their darling Nikolenka; by his relatives as a charming, attractive, and well-mannered young man; and by his acquaintances as a handsome hussar lieutenant, a good dancer, and one of the best catches in the city.

The Rostovs knew everyone in Moscow. The old count had enough money that year, since all his estates had been remortgaged, so Nicholas — having acquired his own racing horse, the most fashionable riding breeches (a style no one else in Moscow had yet), and the latest boots with sharply pointed toes and small silver spurs — had a very good time. After a short period of readjusting to civilian life, Nicholas found it quite pleasant to be home again. He felt that he had grown up and matured considerably. His old despair over failing a Scripture exam, borrowing money from Gavril to pay a sleigh driver, secretly kissing Sonya — he now looked back on all of it as childishness he had left far behind. Now he was a lieutenant of hussars in a silver-braided jacket, wearing the Cross of St. George — a medal awarded for bravery in combat — and he was training a racing horse with well-known, older, respected horsemen. He had a lady acquaintance on one of the boulevards whom he visited in the evenings. He led the mazurka at the Arkharovs' ball, discussed the war with Field Marshal Kamenski, frequented the English Club, and was on friendly terms with a forty-year-old colonel to whom Denisov had introduced him.

His passion for the Emperor had cooled somewhat in Moscow. Still, since he didn't see him and had no opportunity to, he often spoke about him and about his devotion, hinting that he hadn't told everything — that there was something in his feelings for the Emperor that not everyone could understand. With his whole heart he shared the adoration then common in Moscow for the Emperor, who was referred to as "the angel incarnate."

During Rostov's short stay in Moscow before returning to the army, he didn't grow closer to Sonya — if anything, he drifted away from her. She was very pretty and sweet, and clearly deeply in love with him, but he was at that age when there seems to be so much to do that there's no time for love, and a young man values his freedom, which he needs for so many other things. When he thought of Sonya, he told himself, "There will be plenty of girls like her — girls I haven't even met yet. There'll be time enough to think about love when I want to, but right now I have no time." Besides, the company of women struck him as somehow beneath his manhood. He went to balls and into ladies' society while making a show of doing it reluctantly. The races, the English Club, drinking bouts with Denisov, and visits to a certain house — that was a different matter entirely, and perfectly fitting for a dashing young hussar!
At the beginning of March, old Count Ilya Rostov was consumed with arranging a dinner in honor of Prince Bagration at the English Club.

The count paced the hall in his dressing gown, issuing orders to the club steward and to the famous Feoktist, the club's head chef, about asparagus, fresh cucumbers, strawberries, veal, and fish for the dinner. The count had been a founding member and committee member of the club. They had entrusted him with organizing the Bagration celebration because few people knew how to put on a lavish, generous feast like he did, and fewer still would be as willing and able to cover shortfalls from their own pocket. The chef and steward listened to his orders with pleased expressions, knowing that under no other management could they so easily skim a handsome profit from a dinner costing several thousand rubles.
"Now remember — cocks' combs in the turtle soup, you hear!"
"Three cold dishes, then?" asked the chef.
The count considered.
"Can't have fewer — yes, three... The mayonnaise, that's one," he said, counting on his fingers.
"Should I order those large sterlets?" asked the steward.

"Yes, we'll have to — they won't sell them for less. Oh dear, I almost forgot — we need another side dish. Good heavens!" he clutched his head. "Who's going to get me the flowers? Dmitri! Hey, Dmitri! Run out to our Moscow estate," he said to the factotum who appeared at his call. "Hurry up and tell Maksim the gardener to put the servants to work. Everything from the hothouses must be brought here, wrapped carefully in felt. I need two hundred pots here by Friday."

After giving several more orders, he was about to go see his "little countess" for a rest when he remembered something else important. He came back, called the chef and steward again, and resumed giving directions. Light footsteps and the clink of spurs sounded at the door, and the young count walked in — handsome, rosy-cheeked, with a dark little mustache, visibly rested and looking sleeker from his comfortable Moscow life.

"Ah, my boy, my head's spinning!" said the old man with a smile, looking slightly embarrassed in front of his son. "If only you'd help a little! I need singers too. I'll have my own orchestra, but should we also bring in the gypsy singers? You military types like that sort of thing."
"Really, Papa, I think Prince Bagration worried less before the Battle of Schon Grabern than you're worrying now," said his son with a smile.
The old count pretended to be offended.
"Easy for you to say — try doing it yourself!"
And the count turned to the chef, who watched the father and son with a shrewd, respectful, and sympathetic expression.
"What are young people coming to these days, eh, Feoktist?" he said. "Laughing at us old fellows!"
"That's right, your excellency. All they have to do is eat a good dinner — but putting it all together and serving it, that's not their department!"

"Exactly!" exclaimed the count, and cheerfully seizing his son by both hands, he cried, "Now I've got you! Take the sleigh and pair right away and go to Bezukhov's. Tell him Count Ilya sent you to ask for strawberries and fresh pineapples. We can't get them from anyone else. He's not there himself, so you'll have to go in and ask the princesses. And from there, head to Razgulyay — the coachman Ipatka knows the way — and find the gypsy Ilyushka, the one who danced at Count Orlov's in a white Cossack coat, and bring him to me."
"And should I bring the gypsy girls along too?" asked Nicholas, laughing. "Oh, dear..."

At that moment, with quiet footsteps and the businesslike, preoccupied, yet meekly pious expression that never left her face, Anna Mikhaylovna entered the hall. Though she found the count in his dressing gown every day, he always became flustered and apologized for his appearance.

"Not at all, my dear count," she said, modestly lowering her eyes. "But I'll go to Bezukhov's myself. Pierre has arrived, and now we can get whatever we need from his hothouses. I need to see him anyway. He's forwarded me a letter from Boris. Thank God, Boris is now on the staff."
The count was delighted that Anna Mikhaylovna was taking one of his errands off his hands, and he ordered the small closed carriage for her.
"Tell Bezukhov to come. I'll put his name on the list. Is his wife with him?" he asked.
Anna Mikhaylovna raised her eyes to the ceiling, and an expression of deep sorrow crossed her face.

"Oh, my dear friend, his situation is very unfortunate," she said. "If what we hear is true, it's terrible. How little we imagined such a thing when we were celebrating his happiness! And such a pure, angelic soul as young Bezukhov! Yes, I feel for him deeply and will try to offer what comfort I can."
"What — what's happened?" asked both the young and old Rostov.
Anna Mikhaylovna sighed deeply.

"Dolokhov — Maria Ivanovna's son," she said in a conspiratorial whisper, "has completely compromised her, they say. Pierre took him in, invited him to stay at his house in Petersburg, and now... she's come here, and that daredevil followed her!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, intending to show sympathy for Pierre, but betraying through her tone and a half-smile that her sympathies lay partly with the "daredevil," as she called Dolokhov. "They say Pierre is absolutely devastated."
"Dear, dear! Still, tell him to come to the club — it'll all blow over. It's going to be an incredible banquet."

The next day, March third, shortly after one o'clock, two hundred and fifty members of the English Club and fifty guests were waiting for the guest of honor and hero of the Austrian campaign, Prince Bagration, to arrive for dinner.

When news of the Battle of Austerlitz first reached Moscow, the city had been stunned. Russians were so accustomed to victories that when they heard of the defeat, some simply refused to believe it, while others searched for some extraordinary explanation. At the English Club — where everyone distinguished, important, and well-informed gathered — when the news began arriving in December, no one spoke about the war or the battle, as though everyone had agreed to stay silent. The men who set the tone in conversation — Count Rostopchin, Prince Yuri Dolgorukov, Valuev, Count Markov, and Prince Vyazemski — stopped coming to the club, meeting instead in private homes and intimate circles. Muscovites who took their cues from others — Ilya Rostov among them — were left without a clear opinion on the war and without leaders. Everyone felt that something was terribly wrong, and that discussing bad news was difficult, so silence seemed best. But after a while, like a jury emerging from deliberation, the opinion-makers reappeared, and everyone began speaking clearly and with conviction. Explanations were found for the incredible, unprecedented, and seemingly impossible event of a Russian defeat, and the same conclusions began circulating in every corner of Moscow. The causes were: Austrian treachery, a failing supply chain, the treachery of the Pole Przhebyshevski and the Frenchman Langeron, Kutuzov's incompetence, and — whispered quietly — the youth and inexperience of the Emperor, who had trusted worthless and insignificant advisers. But the army itself, the Russian army, everyone declared, had been extraordinary and had performed miracles of bravery. The soldiers, officers, and generals were all heroes. But the greatest hero of all was Prince Bagration, who had distinguished himself at Schon Grabern and during the retreat from Austerlitz, where he alone had withdrawn his column intact, holding off an enemy force twice his own size for an entire day. What also made Bagration Moscow's hero of choice was that he had no connections in the city and was a stranger there. In honoring him, they were paying tribute to a simple fighting Russian soldier without political connections or intrigues — a man associated through the Italian campaign with the great name of Suvorov. Moreover, celebrating Bagration was the perfect way to express disapproval of Kutuzov.

"If there had been no Bagration, it would have been necessary to invent him," said the wit Shinshin, riffing on Voltaire. No one spoke of Kutuzov except a few who cursed him in whispers, calling him a court weathervane and a dirty old man.

All Moscow repeated Prince Dolgorukov's quip: "If you keep kneading and kneading, you're bound to get your hands dirty" — offering the consolation of past victories to soften the present defeat. People also quoted Rostopchin's observation that French soldiers need lofty speeches to drive them into battle, Germans need logical arguments proving it's more dangerous to run away than to advance, but Russian soldiers simply need to be held back. Everywhere, new stories circulated about individual acts of heroism by Russian officers and soldiers at Austerlitz. One man had saved a regimental standard, another had killed five Frenchmen, a third had loaded five cannons single-handedly. People who didn't know Berg personally told how he had taken his sword in his left hand after being wounded in the right, and pressed forward. Of Bolkonsky, nothing was said, and only those who knew him personally mourned that he had died so young, leaving behind a pregnant wife and an eccentric father.
